words.sense: Knowingly making a false statement while under oath in a legal proceeding.
misconceptions: Assuming a confident or accurate retelling becomes firsthand evidence.
Missing that perjury requires a knowingly false statement under legal oath.

words.sense: An out-of-court statement repeated or presented as evidence that what it says is true.
misconceptions: Treating repeated secondhand claims as deliberate sworn lies.
Missing that perjury requires a knowingly false statement under legal oath.

chains.frame: Which word best describes Fatima’s sworn statement about her rent?

beats.text: Under oath, Fatima told the judge she had paid on Monday, although she knew no payment had been made.
beats.decisive_clue: deliberate false claim while under oath
beats.reason: Deliberate false claim while under oath. Knowingly making a false statement while under oath in a legal proceeding.

beats.text: Her statement was only six words long.
beats.decisive_clue: a short statement can still be a knowing falsehood under oath
beats.reason: A short statement can still be a knowing falsehood under oath. Knowingly making a false statement while under oath in a legal proceeding.

chains.feedback_short: A short statement can still be a knowing falsehood under oath.
chains.feedback_deep: Perjury means knowingly making a false statement while under oath in a legal proceeding; hearsay means an out-of-court statement repeated or presented as evidence that what it says is true. Here, deliberate false claim while under oath. The new detail does not change the deciding fact: a short statement can still be a knowing falsehood under oath. Thus perjury remains the stronger choice.
chains.contrast_rule: Perjury lies under oath; hearsay repeats another person’s claim as proof.
